Recaps, history, and books

Your year on the water, brought back to life.

A single trip tells you about one day. A year shows you where you kept going, what you caught, who came along, and how your time on the water changed with the seasons. Then you can turn it into something you keep on a shelf.

Annual recaps

The year you actually had.

Most of a fishing year disappears. You hold on to the big fish and the bad weather, and the rest blurs into "a good summer." A yearly recap brings the whole thing back in one sitting.

See the trips you took and the months you took them. The species that showed up and the ones that did not. The water you returned to most. The people who were there. The photos you had already forgotten. The days that turned out to matter more than they seemed at the time.

There is no rank and no winner here. Your year is not being measured against anyone else's, or against last year's. It is just yours, laid out so you can see it.

Trip recaps

When a day is done, see it as a day. The catches in the order they happened, the photos, the notes you wrote on the drive home, the conditions, the people, the route you covered. It is the difference between a list of fish and remembering the morning.

Yearly recaps

Once a year, everything you recorded comes back together. Trips, catches, species, places, people, photos, maps, and the small statistics that turn out to be more interesting than you expect: how early you started, how late you kept going, the month you barely fished and the month you could not stay off the water.

Highlights are the days that stood out, not the days that scored highest. A first fish for someone. The trip where the boat would not start. The morning you wrote three paragraphs because you did not want to forget it.

Calendar history

A calendar shows the rhythm of a year in a way a list never will. The busy stretches, the long gaps, the season you got out every chance you had, the winter you did not. You can see your own habits without having to count anything.

The places you return to

Some water becomes yours over time. Your history shows which places you keep choosing, how often, and in what months, along with every trip that happened there. A place stops being a pin on a map and becomes a run of days.

Species over time

See what you have caught across a season or across years. Where certain fish tend to show up, when they tend to show up, and what you were using at the time. Useful for planning next spring. Also just good to look at.

The people in your fishing life

Some of your best trips are really about who was with you. Look back at the days you spent with a parent, a partner, a kid, a sibling, or the one friend who always answers the phone at 4 a.m. Watching those days add up over a few years is its own reward.

Photos, back where they belong

Photos from a trip stay with the trip. Not stranded in a camera roll between grocery lists and screenshots, but attached to the place, the date, the fish, and what you wrote that day. Years later they still make sense.

Maps and routes you can revisit

Look back at where trips took you. Optional recorded routes and catch locations stay part of your history, so you can see the shoreline you walked or the water you covered long after you would have stopped remembering it.

Your own patterns

Over enough trips, patterns turn up on their own. The hours you tend to do well. The conditions you keep noting. The bait you come back to. None of it is a score, and none of it is compared to anyone else. It is your record telling you something about your own fishing.

Fishing photo books

A year of trips, catches, photos, places, and notes can become a keepsake photo book. Pages that follow your season the way it happened, with the details you recorded at the time still attached.

Cast Your Line builds the book and saves it as a PDF. The printing is up to you: run it off at home, or take the file to a print shop and get something bound. Keep one for the shelf. Give one to the person who was there, or to someone who will want it long after the trips are over.

This is where a well kept journal ends up, and it is a good reason to keep the journal well.

Worth more every year

The first month of entries is handy. The fifth year is something else. Trips you would have forgotten, people who have moved away, water that has changed, a kid who was small in those photos. The longer you keep it, the more there is to come back to.

Which is the whole point. You are not filling in a database. You are keeping your fishing life.
